texts.16:
## Deimos (Mars II)
Deimos is the smaller and outer of the two natural satellites of Mars with a mean radius of 6.2 km. It takes 30.3 hours to orbit Mars at an orbital velocity of 1.35 km/s. It has an escape velocity of 5.6 m/s and apparent magnitude of 12.45. Like most bodies of its size, Deimos is highly non-spherical with triaxial dimensions of 15×12.2×11 km making it 0.56 times the size of Phobos. It orbits 23,460 km distant from Mars.
Deimos, like Phobos, has spectra, albedos and densities similar to those of a C- or D-type asteroid. It is composed of rock rich in carbonaceous material, much like C-type asteroids and carbonaceous chondrite meteorites. It is cratered, but the surface is noticeably smoother than that of Phobos, caused by the partial filling of craters with regolith. The regolith is highly porous and has a radar-estimated density of only 1.471 g/cm 3.
Only two geological features on Deimos have been given names. They are the two largest craters, _Swift_ (at 12.5°N 358.2°W, diameter 1000 m, named after _Jonathan Swift_ the author of _Gulliver’s Travels_) and _Voltaire_ (at 22°N 3.5°W, diameter 1900 m, “Voltaire” was the _nom-de-plume_ of _François-Marie Arouet_). The two craters are named after writers who speculated on the existence of two Martian moons before Phobos and Deimos were discovered.
_Deimos photographed in colour in 2009 by Mars Reconnaisance Orbiter._
Deimos’s orbit is nearly circular and is close to Mars’s equatorial plane. Because the orbit is relatively close to Mars and has only a very small inclination to Mars’s equator, it cannot be seen from Martian latitudes greater than 82.7°. It is possibly an asteroid that was perturbed by _Jupiter_ into an orbit that allowed it to be captured by Mars, though this hypothesis is disputed.
texts.17:
## Deimos (Mars II)
_A high-resolution view of Deimos from 30 km, taken by the_ Viking 2 Orbiter _in 1977._
Unlike Phobos, which orbits so fast that it actually rises in the west and sets in the east, Deimos rises in the east and sets in the west. However, the Sun-synodic orbital period of Deimos of about 30.4 hours exceeds the Martian solar day (“sol”) of about 24.7 hours by such a small amount that 2.7 days elapse between its rising and setting for an equatorial observer.
This [left] is one of the highest-resolution images ever taken from an orbiting or flyby spacecraft. The image covers an area of 1.2 km by 1.5 km and features as small as 3 metres across can be seen. Note that many of the craters are covered over by a layer of regolith estimated to be about 50 metres thick. Large blocks, 10 to 30 metres across, are also visible. North is at 11:30.

## Comet Siding Spring at Mars
The comet image shown here is a composite of Hubble exposures taken between 18 th October 2013 8:06 a.m. EDT and 19 th October 11:17 p.m. EDT. Hubble took a separate photograph of Mars at 10:37 p.m. EDT on 18 th October.
The Mars and comet images have been added together to create a single picture to illustrate the angular separation, or distance, between the comet and Mars at closest approach. The separation is approximately 1.5 arc minutes, or one-twentieth of the angular diameter of the full Moon. The background star field in this composite image is synthesized from ground-based telescope data provided by the Palomar Digital Sky Survey, which has been reprocessed to approximate Hubble’s resolution. The solid icy comet nucleus is too small to be resolved in the Hubble picture. The comet’s bright coma, a diffuse cloud of dust enshrouding the nucleus, and a dusty tail, are clearly visible.
This is a composite image because a single exposure of the stellar background, comet Siding Spring, and Mars would be problematic. Mars is actually 10,000 times brighter than the comet, and so could not be properly exposed to show detail in the Planet. The comet and Mars were also moving with respect to each other and so could not be imaged simultaneously in one exposure without one of the objects being motion blurred. Hubble had to be programmed to track on the comet and Mars separately in two different observations.
[Image: NASA, ESA, PSI, JHU/APL, STScI/AURA] The images were taken with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3.
Mars (tracking from right to left) and Comet Siding Spring crossed paths on 19 th October 2013.
The comet, estimated to have a nucleus 700 m in size, passed Mars at approximately 87,000 miles (about one-third of the distance between Earth and the Moon) at 2:28 p.m. EDT on 19 th October 2014. At that time, the comet and Mars were approximately 149 million miles from Earth.
The comet is on its first visit to the inner Solar System from the Oort cloud and in common with such objects its behaviour is notoriously difficult to predict.
texts.19:
## Comet Siding Spring at Mars
_This animation of comet_ C/2013 A1 Siding Spring _was captured by the_ Mast Camera _(Mastcam) on_ Curiosity Mars rover _as the comet passed near the planet on 19 th October 2014_
The animation consists of 10 exposures of 25 seconds each, taken between 21:33 UT and 00:34 UT on 20 th October. The exposures are projected onto a celestial frame. The still is an image from the animation. Most of the specks are electronic noise. The short, straight streaks are stars.
Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/TAMU with enhancements by [Astronomy Now’s Greg Smye-Rumsby]
Comet Siding Spring’s close shave by Mars provided a rare glimpse into how Oort Cloud comets behave, according to new research. The comet flew by Mars at a range of just 135,000 kilometres – close enough for the outer ridges of its tenuous atmosphere to pummel the planet with gas and dust. In just a short flyby, the comet dumped about 1,000 to 2,000 kg of dust made of magnesium, silicon, calcium and potassium – all of which are rock-forming elements – into the upper atmosphere, the new study found.

## Discovery and etymology
[edit]
Asaph Hall III, discoverer of Deimos
Deimos was discovered by Asaph Hall at the United States Naval Observatory in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), on 12 August 1877, at about 07:48 UTC.[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-20) Hall, who also discovered Phobos shortly afterwards, had been specifically searching for Martian moons at the time.
The moon is named after Deimos, a figure representing dread in Greek mythology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-Blunck-21) The name was suggested by academic Henry Madan, who drew from Book XV of the _Iliad_, where Ares (Greek counterpart of the Roman god Mars) summons Dread (Deimos) and Fear (Phobos).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-22)
Planetary moons other than Earth's were never given symbols in the astronomical literature. Denis Moskowitz, a software engineer who designed most of the dwarf planet symbols, proposed a Greek delta (the initial of Deimos) combined with Mars's spear as the symbol of Deimos (). This symbol is not widely used.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-moons-23)
The origin of Mars's moons is unknown and the hypotheses are controversial.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-burns-24) The main hypotheses are that they formed either by capture or by accretion.

## Discovery and etymology
Because of the postulated similarity to the composition of C- or D-type asteroids, one hypothesis is that the moons may be objects captured into Martian orbit from the asteroid belt, with orbits that have been circularized either by atmospheric drag or tidal forces,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-cazenave-25) as capture requires dissipation of energy. The current Martian atmosphere is too thin to capture a Phobos-sized object by atmospheric braking.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-burns-24)Geoffrey Landis has pointed out that the capture could have occurred if the original body was a binary asteroid that separated due to tidal forces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-landis-26) The main alternative hypothesis is that the moons accreted in the present position. Another hypothesis is that Mars was once surrounded by many Phobos- and Deimos-sized bodies, perhaps ejected into orbit around it by a collision with a planetesimal.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-27)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-28)
In 2021, Amirhossein Bagheri (ETH Zurich), Amir Khan (ETH Zurich), Michael Efroimsky (US Naval Observatory) and their colleagues proposed a new hypothesis on the origin of the moons. By analyzing the seismic and orbital data from the Mars InSight Mission and other missions, they proposed that the moons were born from the disruption of a common parent body around 1 to 2.7 billion years ago. The common progenitor of Phobos and Deimos was most probably hit by another object and shattered to form Phobos and Deimos.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-29)

## Physical characteristics
[edit]
Size comparison between Phobos, Deimos and the Moon (right)
Deimos is a gray-colored body. Like most bodies of its size, Deimos is highly non-spherical with triaxial dimensions of 16.1 km ×11.8 km ×10.2 km (10.0 mi ×7.3 mi ×6.3 mi), corresponding to a mean diameter of 12.5 km (7.8 mi) which makes it about 57% the size of Phobos.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-Ernst2023-7) Deimos is composed of rock rich in carbonaceous material, much like C-type asteroids and carbonaceous chondrite meteorites.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-30) It is cratered, but the surface is noticeably smoother than that of Phobos, caused by the partial filling of craters with regolith._[citation needed_] The regolith is highly porous and has a radar-estimated density of only 1.471 g/cm 3.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-Michaelbusch-31)
The escape velocity from Deimos is 5.6 m/s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-NASA-6) The apparent magnitude of Deimos is 12.45.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-JPLSSD-32)

## Orbital characteristics
[edit]
Orbits of Phobos and Deimos (to scale)
Deimos's orbit is nearly circular and is close to Mars's equatorial plane. Deimos is possibly an asteroid that was perturbed by Jupiter into an orbit that allowed it to be captured by Mars, though this hypothesis is still controversial and disputed.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-burns-24) Both Deimos and Phobos have very circular orbits which lie almost exactly in Mars's equatorial plane, and hence a capture origin requires a mechanism for circularizing the initially highly eccentric orbit, and adjusting its inclination into the equatorial plane, most likely by a combination of atmospheric drag and tidal forces;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-cazenave-25) it is not clear that sufficient time was available for this to have occurred for Deimos.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-burns-24)

As seen from Mars, Deimos would have an angular diameter of no more than 2.5 minutes (sixty minutes make one degree), one twelfth of the width of the Moon as seen from Earth, and would therefore appear almost star-like to the naked eye.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon)#cite_note-richardson-35) At its brightest ("full moon") it would be about as bright as Venus is from Earth; at the first- or third-quarter phase it would be about as bright as Vega. Heights are each moon’s average distance from its planet’s center minus the planet’s average radius, our calculation from NASA’s fact sheets.[[1]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-1)[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2)[[3]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-3)[[4]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-4)[[5]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-5)[[7]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-7)

## How does Deimos orbit Mars?
**Deimos circles Mars once every 30 h 18 min, about 20,000 km (12,000 mi) above the surface, on a nearly circular path close to Mars’s equator.**[[3]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-3)[[8]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-8) Mars spins once every 24.6 hours, so Deimos moves only a little slower than the ground beneath it.[[3]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-3) From the surface it rises in the east and sets in the west, like our Moon.[[7]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-7) But it creeps: Astronomy magazine calculates that it stays above the horizon for about 60 hours at a time.[[9]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-9)
Deimos turns once per orbit, so it always shows Mars the same face.[[3]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-3)[[11]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-11) And while Phobos is moving closer to Mars, Deimos is moving away from it, ESA says.[[10]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-10)
Its orbit is known well, but not perfectly. The first time a rover tried to catch Deimos crossing the Sun, the moon was 40 km (25 mi) from where scientists expected, NASA said in 2019. Each new sighting tightens the numbers.[[12]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-12) In February 2022, ESA’s Mars Express watched Deimos pass in front of Jupiter and its four largest moons, which pinned down its position more precisely.[[10]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-10)

## Why is Deimos so smooth?
**Because a thick blanket of loose dust and broken rock, called regolith, covers it and partly fills some of its craters.**[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2)[[13]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-13) NASA says this layer may be as deep as 100 m (328 ft). Most of Deimos’s craters are smaller than 2.5 km (1.6 mi) across, and it has none of the grooves and ridges that cross Phobos.[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2)
Deimos’s gravity is too weak to hold the dust that impacts throw up. NASA says Mars’s gravity keeps that debris in a ring near Deimos’s orbit, and the moon sweeps it back up over time.[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2) Pictures taken in 2009 by the HiRISE camera on NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter show the smoothest areas are the reddest. Fresh craters are less red, probably because their material has spent less time exposed to space.[[13]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-13)
A study published in Nature Astronomy on Aug 18,2026, offers one explanation for both the dust and Deimos’s biggest feature: a basin about 10 km (6 mi) wide around its south pole. Its simulations show that an asteroid about 320 m (1,050 ft) wide, hitting at a slant, could have carved the basin without breaking Deimos apart. The debris it threw out buried older craters, more than 200 m (660 ft) deep in places.[[14]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-14)[[15]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-15) The study also finds Deimos highly porous inside, resembling the loose “rubble-pile” asteroids that spacecraft have visited.[[15]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-15)

## Why is Deimos so smooth?
Only two features on Deimos have official names: the craters Swift, about 1 km (0.6 mi) across, and Voltaire, about 1.9 km (1.2 mi). The International Astronomical Union adopted both names in 1973.[[16]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-16)[[17]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-17) Craters on Deimos are named for authors who wrote about Mars’s moons, such as Jonathan Swift, who wrote “Gulliver’s Travels.”[[16]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-16)[[18]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-18)

## Where did Deimos come from?
**Nobody knows yet.** There are two leading ideas. Mars may have captured a passing asteroid, which would explain why Deimos looks like a dark, carbon-rich asteroid. Or Deimos may have formed from debris thrown into orbit when something huge hit Mars, which better fits its circular orbit over Mars’s equator.[[8]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-8)[[19]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-19)
Recent results point different ways:
*   **2023:** The Emirates Mars Mission’s Hope orbiter, run by the United Arab Emirates, flew within about 100 km (60 mi) of Deimos. Its team said the moon’s infrared signature looks more like basaltic Mars than a D-type asteroid, and points to “a planetary origin.”[[20]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-20)  
*   **2024:** A NASA-led study in the journal Icarus proposed a third route: an asteroid torn apart by Mars’s gravity, with its fragments settling into a disk that could have built both moons. That would put more moon-building material out where Deimos orbits. A giant impact leaves most of its debris close to the planet.[[8]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-8)  
*   **2026:** The Nature Astronomy impact study found Deimos built like a rubble pile. ESA’s Hera project scientist Michael Kueppers said that “does not necessarily mean the moon is in fact a captured asteroid.”[[14]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-14)

## Who has photographed Deimos up close?
**Few spacecraft get close, because Deimos orbits far beyond where most Mars **Orbiter**An orbiter circles Mars without landing, studying the planet from above - and many also relay rover data back to Earth.More in the glossary fly.**[[14]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-14)[[20]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-20)
*   **1970s:** NASA’s Viking orbiters found Deimos smoother and dustier than heavily cratered Phobos.[[14]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-14)  
*   **Feb 21,2009:** HiRISE took color-enhanced views showing details as small as about 60 m (197 ft).[[13]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-13)  
*   **2023:** Hope made repeated flybys, the closest at about 100 km (60 mi), the nearest any spacecraft had come since Viking in 1977. It made the first extreme and far ultraviolet observations of Deimos, and studied parts of its far side whose makeup had never been examined.[[20]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-20)  
*   **Mar 12,2025:** ESA’s Hera asteroid mission flew past Mars and imaged Deimos from about 1,000 km (620 mi). It saw the side that faces away from Mars, which is rarely seen.[[11]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-11)[[21]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-21) Its thermal camera, supplied by JAXA, showed Deimos warmer than Mars’s surface, because its pitch-black surface soaks up sunlight.[[22]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-22)

## What does Deimos look like from Mars?
**A tiny, bright dot that drifts slowly across the night sky.** Astronomy magazine calculates that Deimos appears about 2.5 arcminutes wide, around twice the largest Venus ever looks from Earth. It is usually invisible by day, but at night it outshines every star.[[9]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-9)
Mars’s **Rover**A rover is a robot vehicle that drives across Mars, following plans its team on Earth sends ahead of each drive.More in the glossary have photographed it many times. Spirit caught both moons crossing the night sky on Aug 30,2005.[[7]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-7)Curiosity watched Deimos cross the face of the Sun on Mar 17,2019. Deimos covers so little of the Sun that scientists call that a transit, not an eclipse. By April 2019, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity had recorded eight Deimos transits.[[12]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-12)
On Mar 1,2025, at 4:27 a.m. local time, Perseverance’s navigation camera combined 16 long exposures, about 52 seconds in all, to catch Deimos shining before dawn. The stars Regulus and Algieba show up in the same frame.[[23]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-23)

## How did Deimos get its name?
**From Greek myth: Deimos means dread.** Asaph Hall discovered Deimos on Aug 11,1877, six days before Phobos, at the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, D.C.[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2)[[5]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-5)[[6]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-6) He named both moons for the sons of Ares, the Greek counterpart of the Roman war god Mars. NASA translates Deimos as dread; ESA gives terror or panic.[[2]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-2)[[6]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-6)

## MMX: the next visit to Deimos
**Japan’s MMX plans to observe Deimos as well as land on Phobos.** It launched on an H3 rocket from Tanegashima on **Oct 20,2026, at 04:41 Japan time** (Oct 19, 19:41 UTC).[[25]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-25)[[26]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-26) It should reach Mars in 2027 and spend about three years there. It plans to study Phobos, collect samples from its surface and observe Deimos, then bring the samples to Earth in Japan’s fiscal 2031.[[24]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-24) The 2026 impact study made predictions about Deimos that MMX can test.[[14]](https://marsprogress.com/mars/moons/deimos/#src-14)

## Phobos (Mars I)
See also the Phobos spacecraft programme by the USSR.

## Deimos (Mars II)
Deimos is the smaller and outer of the two natural satellites of Mars with a mean radius of 6.2 km. It takes 30.3 hours to orbit Mars at an orbital velocity of 1.35 km/s. It has an escape velocity of 5.6 m/s and apparent magnitude of 12.45. Like most bodies of its size, Deimos is highly non-spherical with triaxial dimensions of 15×12.2×11 km making it 0.56 times the size of Phobos. It orbits 23,460 km distant from Mars.
Deimos, like Phobos, has spectra, albedos and densities similar to those of a C- or D-type asteroid. It is composed of rock rich in carbonaceous material, much like C-type asteroids and carbonaceous chondrite meteorites. It is cratered, but the surface is noticeably smoother than that of Phobos, caused by the partial filling of craters with regolith. The regolith is highly porous and has a radar-estimated density of only 1.471 g/cm 3.
Only two geological features on Deimos have been given names. They are the two largest craters, _Swift_ (at 12.5°N 358.2°W, diameter 1000 m, named after _Jonathan Swift_ the author of _Gulliver’s Travels_) and _Voltaire_ (at 22°N 3.5°W, diameter 1900 m, “Voltaire” was the _nom-de-plume_ of _François-Marie Arouet_). The two craters are named after writers who speculated on the existence of two Martian moons before Phobos and Deimos were discovered.
_Deimos photographed in colour in 2009 by Mars Reconnaisance Orbiter._
Deimos’s orbit is nearly circular and is close to Mars’s equatorial plane. Because the orbit is relatively close to Mars and has only a very small inclination to Mars’s equator, it cannot be seen from Martian latitudes greater than 82.7°. It is possibly an asteroid that was perturbed by _Jupiter_ into an orbit that allowed it to be captured by Mars, though this hypothesis is disputed.

## Deimos (Mars II)
_A high-resolution view of Deimos from 30 km, taken by the_ Viking 2 Orbiter _in 1977._
Unlike Phobos, which orbits so fast that it actually rises in the west and sets in the east, Deimos rises in the east and sets in the west. However, the Sun-synodic orbital period of Deimos of about 30.4 hours exceeds the Martian solar day (“sol”) of about 24.7 hours by such a small amount that 2.7 days elapse between its rising and setting for an equatorial observer.
This [left] is one of the highest-resolution images ever taken from an orbiting or flyby spacecraft. The image covers an area of 1.2 km by 1.5 km and features as small as 3 metres across can be seen. Note that many of the craters are covered over by a layer of regolith estimated to be about 50 metres thick. Large blocks, 10 to 30 metres across, are also visible. North is at 11:30.

## Comet Siding Spring at Mars
The comet image shown here is a composite of Hubble exposures taken between 18 th October 2013 8:06 a.m. EDT and 19 th October 11:17 p.m. EDT. Hubble took a separate photograph of Mars at 10:37 p.m. EDT on 18 th October.
The Mars and comet images have been added together to create a single picture to illustrate the angular separation, or distance, between the comet and Mars at closest approach. The separation is approximately 1.5 arc minutes, or one-twentieth of the angular diameter of the full Moon. The background star field in this composite image is synthesized from ground-based telescope data provided by the Palomar Digital Sky Survey, which has been reprocessed to approximate Hubble’s resolution. The solid icy comet nucleus is too small to be resolved in the Hubble picture. The comet’s bright coma, a diffuse cloud of dust enshrouding the nucleus, and a dusty tail, are clearly visible.
This is a composite image because a single exposure of the stellar background, comet Siding Spring, and Mars would be problematic. Mars is actually 10,000 times brighter than the comet, and so could not be properly exposed to show detail in the Planet. The comet and Mars were also moving with respect to each other and so could not be imaged simultaneously in one exposure without one of the objects being motion blurred. Hubble had to be programmed to track on the comet and Mars separately in two different observations.
[Image: NASA, ESA, PSI, JHU/APL, STScI/AURA] The images were taken with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3.
Mars (tracking from right to left) and Comet Siding Spring crossed paths on 19 th October 2013.
The comet, estimated to have a nucleus 700 m in size, passed Mars at approximately 87,000 miles (about one-third of the distance between Earth and the Moon) at 2:28 p.m. EDT on 19 th October 2014. At that time, the comet and Mars were approximately 149 million miles from Earth.
The comet is on its first visit to the inner Solar System from the Oort cloud and in common with such objects its behaviour is notoriously difficult to predict.

## Comet Siding Spring at Mars
_This animation of comet_ C/2013 A1 Siding Spring _was captured by the_ Mast Camera _(Mastcam) on_ Curiosity Mars rover _as the comet passed near the planet on 19 th October 2014_
The animation consists of 10 exposures of 25 seconds each, taken between 21:33 UT and 00:34 UT on 20 th October. The exposures are projected onto a celestial frame. The still is an image from the animation. Most of the specks are electronic noise. The short, straight streaks are stars.
Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/TAMU with enhancements by [Astronomy Now’s Greg Smye-Rumsby]
Comet Siding Spring’s close shave by Mars provided a rare glimpse into how Oort Cloud comets behave, according to new research. The comet flew by Mars at a range of just 135,000 kilometres – close enough for the outer ridges of its tenuous atmosphere to pummel the planet with gas and dust. In just a short flyby, the comet dumped about 1,000 to 2,000 kg of dust made of magnesium, silicon, calcium and potassium – all of which are rock-forming elements – into the upper atmosphere, the new study found.

**Lucian** is a tiny lunarimpact crater that is located in the northeastern part of the Mare Tranquillitatis. It was named in 1973 after 2nd century Greek writer Lucian of Samosata.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_(crater)#cite_note-2) The nearest named craters are Lyell to the east-southeast, Theophrastus to the northeast and Gardner to the north-northeast. A little farther to the north is Maraldi crater. Lucian was previously designated Maraldi B.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_(crater)#cite_note-Moore_Rees_2014-3)
This is a circular, cone-shaped formation with a negligible interior floor. It has not been significantly degraded by impact erosion.

Title: A Name for each Crater
Chunks: 6,7,8,9,10
It was decided that in Mars craters would be given the names of dead scientists or of writers who had contributed to the popularisation of Mars, like Schiaperelli or H.G. Wells. Towns under 100.000 inhabitants would be the source for the names of the smaller craters. The larger valleys would be named using the name of Mars in different languages, while smaller valleys would be named after rivers from the Earth. No feature under 100 metres would be given an official name unless it was of an exceptional scientific interest.
Within the Catalan speaking-area we find the craters Comàs Solà, with a diameter of 127 km; Isil, with 82 km, after the small town of Les Valls d’Àneu, in Pallars Sobirà. We also find valleys named Iberus Vallis (after river Ebro) or Tader Valles (after river Segura).
However, the arrival in Mars of the explorer robots Spirit and Opportunity in 2004 forced the members of the group to use unofficial names for the smaller craters or rocks studied — Sponge Bob, Abba or Bee Gees, for instance.
VENUS, THE PLANET OF WOMEN
In Venus, the dense atmosphere hinders direct observation of the surface from the Earth. The 300 metre radiotelescope in Arecibo, however, got to find two new very reflective areas —Alpha and Beta Regio— and a bright area— Maxwell Montes. Up until the arrival of the mission Magellan —which had the task of studiying its atmosphere and mapping its surface— nothing else was known. Between 1990 and 1992 the on-board radar got to map 98% of its surface, covered a great deal by volcanic materials and structures. A lot of volcanos were found, but, in contrast to the Moon, very few impact craters. Its surface, therefore, is young and continually renewed with not too viscous lava flows that run through channels of planetary dimensions.

It had to be created a new working group in the IAU for the new geological structures without a name which asked for international collaboration. Since Venus is the goddess of beauty, it was decided that its geographical features would be given names related to goddesses (fertility, war, beauty, etc.). Craters larger than 20 km, however, would be named after dead women who contributed greatly to their working fields. Common women names would be used for smaller craters.
Famous women from Castille, like Isabella “the Catholic queen” or the physician and educator from the 15th century Beatriz Galindo —known as La Latina, are also acknowledged and have their names given to a crater. The only woman from the Catalan speaking-area we find is the Spanish dancing dancer from Barcelona Carmen Amaya, very well-knwon in the USA, where appeared in some films and even danced for president Roosevelt.![Image 6: 24A-73](blob:http://localhost/4c684bb7fe0687c6d8f7608e885c62cb)
© Carles Duarte i Montserrat
Crater Endymion, Selene’s lover, on the north-eastern part of the Moon.  
«In Mars we find the craters Comàs Solà, with a diameter of 127 km; Isil, with 82 km, after the small town of Les Valls d’Àneu, in Pallars Sobirà. We also find valleys named Iberus Vallis (after river Ebro) or Tader Valles (after river Segura)»  
![Image 7: 26-73](blob:http://localhost/e617212a66ffbe2eb8709106691d65ab)
© NASA
Caloris Basin in Mercury, close to the Ausiàs March crater.  
A MATTER OF NAMES

Planets are named after the main Roman gods. In order to give a name to the elements of the geography of the planets we only have to extend the tradition to the relationship among the gods or use the names of equivalent gods of other cultures. However, this source is limited. We have to look for other sources. This is the case of Miranda, one of Uranus’ satellites, daughter of the duke Prospero from The Tempest, by William Shakespeare. Its geogrpahical features’ names honour the characters and towns of Shakespeare’s work.
The probe Mariner 10 flew over Mercury three times between 1974 and 1975. Its images revealed a planet full of impact craters, similar to the Moon. It was in 1973 when the IAU created the Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature (WGPSN). There were created working subgroups for each planet or satellite. The conclusions of each of the groups, if aproved by the WGPSN, had to be confirmed by the general assembly of the IAU, which was held every two years.
The group in charge of Mercury was directed by David Morrison— investigator of the NASA Astrobiolocal Institute, who was internationally known. As he himself told in an interview to the e-journal Cabinet in 2007, the aim of creating a database of names with an international representation was achieved in less than a year.
Currently, David Morrison, already retired, is the director of the Carl Sagan Center from the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence Institute (SETI) in California. At the beginning of October 2011, the journal Vilaweb had an interview with him. «We thought of a wide range of possibilities for the names of the impact craters; from great astronomers to birds. In the maps of the Moon and Mars astronomers and scientists are honoured, and I defended that we had to break away from that tradition and name the main craters in Mercury after people from the world of the arts and literature —authors, painters, sculptors, poets, architects, etc.» But the working group didn’t know enough about these fields, «especially from an international perspective», and Morrison explained that «that is why reference works and univeristy researchers had to be consulted in order to elaborate a list of possible names».

In 1979 the group lead by Morrison aproved the incorporation of the name of Ausiàs March to the list, but said: «I don’t remember who suggested Ausiàs March, but all in the group recognised it was a good suggestion as an important writer of the Catalan language». As confesed to Jennifer Blue, from the USGS, answering to why the name of Ausiàs March for the crater, « I wanted to be sure of having Catalan and Castilian writers represented in the craters of Mercury».

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Lucian
Lunar Orbiter 4 image  
Coordinates14°20′N 36°47′E / 14.34°N 36.78°E  
Diameter6.85 km (4.26 mi)  
Depth1.6 km (0.99 mi)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_(crater)#cite_note-1)  
Colongitude324° at sunrise  
EponymLucian
Oblique view from Apollo 15
**Lucian** is a tiny lunarimpact crater that is located in the northeastern part of the Mare Tranquillitatis. It was named in 1973 after 2nd century Greek writer Lucian of Samosata.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_(crater)#cite_note-2) The nearest named craters are Lyell to the east-southeast, Theophrastus to the northeast and Gardner to the north-northeast. A little farther to the north is Maraldi crater. Lucian was previously designated Maraldi B.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_(crater)#cite_note-Moore_Rees_2014-3)
This is a circular, cone-shaped formation with a negligible interior floor. It has not been significantly degraded by impact erosion.

texts.6:
It was decided that in Mars craters would be given the names of dead scientists or of writers who had contributed to the popularisation of Mars, like Schiaperelli or H.G. Wells. Towns under 100.000 inhabitants would be the source for the names of the smaller craters. The larger valleys would be named using the name of Mars in different languages, while smaller valleys would be named after rivers from the Earth. No feature under 100 metres would be given an official name unless it was of an exceptional scientific interest.
Within the Catalan speaking-area we find the craters Comàs Solà, with a diameter of 127 km; Isil, with 82 km, after the small town of Les Valls d’Àneu, in Pallars Sobirà. We also find valleys named Iberus Vallis (after river Ebro) or Tader Valles (after river Segura).
However, the arrival in Mars of the explorer robots Spirit and Opportunity in 2004 forced the members of the group to use unofficial names for the smaller craters or rocks studied — Sponge Bob, Abba or Bee Gees, for instance.
VENUS, THE PLANET OF WOMEN
In Venus, the dense atmosphere hinders direct observation of the surface from the Earth. The 300 metre radiotelescope in Arecibo, however, got to find two new very reflective areas —Alpha and Beta Regio— and a bright area— Maxwell Montes. Up until the arrival of the mission Magellan —which had the task of studiying its atmosphere and mapping its surface— nothing else was known. Between 1990 and 1992 the on-board radar got to map 98% of its surface, covered a great deal by volcanic materials and structures. A lot of volcanos were found, but, in contrast to the Moon, very few impact craters. Its surface, therefore, is young and continually renewed with not too viscous lava flows that run through channels of planetary dimensions.
texts.7:
It had to be created a new working group in the IAU for the new geological structures without a name which asked for international collaboration. Since Venus is the goddess of beauty, it was decided that its geographical features would be given names related to goddesses (fertility, war, beauty, etc.). Craters larger than 20 km, however, would be named after dead women who contributed greatly to their working fields. Common women names would be used for smaller craters.
Famous women from Castille, like Isabella “the Catholic queen” or the physician and educator from the 15th century Beatriz Galindo —known as La Latina, are also acknowledged and have their names given to a crater. The only woman from the Catalan speaking-area we find is the Spanish dancing dancer from Barcelona Carmen Amaya, very well-knwon in the USA, where appeared in some films and even danced for president Roosevelt.![Image 6: 24A-73](blob:http://localhost/4c684bb7fe0687c6d8f7608e885c62cb)
© Carles Duarte i Montserrat
Crater Endymion, Selene’s lover, on the north-eastern part of the Moon.

Caloris Basin in Mercury, close to the Ausiàs March crater.  
A MATTER OF NAMES
texts.8:
Planets are named after the main Roman gods. In order to give a name to the elements of the geography of the planets we only have to extend the tradition to the relationship among the gods or use the names of equivalent gods of other cultures. However, this source is limited. We have to look for other sources. This is the case of Miranda, one of Uranus’ satellites, daughter of the duke Prospero from The Tempest, by William Shakespeare. Its geogrpahical features’ names honour the characters and towns of Shakespeare’s work.
The probe Mariner 10 flew over Mercury three times between 1974 and 1975. Its images revealed a planet full of impact craters, similar to the Moon. It was in 1973 when the IAU created the Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature (WGPSN). There were created working subgroups for each planet or satellite. The conclusions of each of the groups, if aproved by the WGPSN, had to be confirmed by the general assembly of the IAU, which was held every two years.
The group in charge of Mercury was directed by David Morrison— investigator of the NASA Astrobiolocal Institute, who was internationally known. As he himself told in an interview to the e-journal Cabinet in 2007, the aim of creating a database of names with an international representation was achieved in less than a year.
Currently, David Morrison, already retired, is the director of the Carl Sagan Center from the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence Institute (SETI) in California. At the beginning of October 2011, the journal Vilaweb had an interview with him. «We thought of a wide range of possibilities for the names of the impact craters; from great astronomers to birds. In the maps of the Moon and Mars astronomers and scientists are honoured, and I defended that we had to break away from that tradition and name the main craters in Mercury after people from the world of the arts and literature —authors, painters, sculptors, poets, architects, etc.» But the working group didn’t know enough about these fields, «especially from an international perspective», and Morrison explained that «that is why reference works and univeristy researchers had to be consulted in order to elaborate a list of possible names».

Title: A Name for each Crater
Chunks: 6,7,8,9,10
It was decided that in Mars craters would be given the names of dead scientists or of writers who had contributed to the popularisation of Mars, like Schiaperelli or H.G. Wells. Towns under 100.000 inhabitants would be the source for the names of the smaller craters. The larger valleys would be named using the name of Mars in different languages, while smaller valleys would be named after rivers from the Earth. No feature under 100 metres would be given an official name unless it was of an exceptional scientific interest.
Within the Catalan speaking-area we find the craters Comàs Solà, with a diameter of 127 km; Isil, with 82 km, after the small town of Les Valls d’Àneu, in Pallars Sobirà. We also find valleys named Iberus Vallis (after river Ebro) or Tader Valles (after river Segura).
However, the arrival in Mars of the explorer robots Spirit and Opportunity in 2004 forced the members of the group to use unofficial names for the smaller craters or rocks studied — Sponge Bob, Abba or Bee Gees, for instance.
VENUS, THE PLANET OF WOMEN
In Venus, the dense atmosphere hinders direct observation of the surface from the Earth. The 300 metre radiotelescope in Arecibo, however, got to find two new very reflective areas —Alpha and Beta Regio— and a bright area— Maxwell Montes. Up until the arrival of the mission Magellan —which had the task of studiying its atmosphere and mapping its surface— nothing else was known. Between 1990 and 1992 the on-board radar got to map 98% of its surface, covered a great deal by volcanic materials and structures. A lot of volcanos were found, but, in contrast to the Moon, very few impact craters. Its surface, therefore, is young and continually renewed with not too viscous lava flows that run through channels of planetary dimensions.

It had to be created a new working group in the IAU for the new geological structures without a name which asked for international collaboration. Since Venus is the goddess of beauty, it was decided that its geographical features would be given names related to goddesses (fertility, war, beauty, etc.). Craters larger than 20 km, however, would be named after dead women who contributed greatly to their working fields. Common women names would be used for smaller craters.
Famous women from Castille, like Isabella “the Catholic queen” or the physician and educator from the 15th century Beatriz Galindo —known as La Latina, are also acknowledged and have their names given to a crater. The only woman from the Catalan speaking-area we find is the Spanish dancing dancer from Barcelona Carmen Amaya, very well-knwon in the USA, where appeared in some films and even danced for president Roosevelt.![Image 6: 24A-73](blob:http://localhost/4c684bb7fe0687c6d8f7608e885c62cb)
© Carles Duarte i Montserrat
Crater Endymion, Selene’s lover, on the north-eastern part of the Moon.  
«In Mars we find the craters Comàs Solà, with a diameter of 127 km; Isil, with 82 km, after the small town of Les Valls d’Àneu, in Pallars Sobirà. We also find valleys named Iberus Vallis (after river Ebro) or Tader Valles (after river Segura)»  
![Image 7: 26-73](blob:http://localhost/e617212a66ffbe2eb8709106691d65ab)
© NASA
Caloris Basin in Mercury, close to the Ausiàs March crater.  
A MATTER OF NAMES

Planets are named after the main Roman gods. In order to give a name to the elements of the geography of the planets we only have to extend the tradition to the relationship among the gods or use the names of equivalent gods of other cultures. However, this source is limited. We have to look for other sources. This is the case of Miranda, one of Uranus’ satellites, daughter of the duke Prospero from The Tempest, by William Shakespeare. Its geogrpahical features’ names honour the characters and towns of Shakespeare’s work.
The probe Mariner 10 flew over Mercury three times between 1974 and 1975. Its images revealed a planet full of impact craters, similar to the Moon. It was in 1973 when the IAU created the Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature (WGPSN). There were created working subgroups for each planet or satellite. The conclusions of each of the groups, if aproved by the WGPSN, had to be confirmed by the general assembly of the IAU, which was held every two years.
The group in charge of Mercury was directed by David Morrison— investigator of the NASA Astrobiolocal Institute, who was internationally known. As he himself told in an interview to the e-journal Cabinet in 2007, the aim of creating a database of names with an international representation was achieved in less than a year.
Currently, David Morrison, already retired, is the director of the Carl Sagan Center from the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence Institute (SETI) in California. At the beginning of October 2011, the journal Vilaweb had an interview with him. «We thought of a wide range of possibilities for the names of the impact craters; from great astronomers to birds. In the maps of the Moon and Mars astronomers and scientists are honoured, and I defended that we had to break away from that tradition and name the main craters in Mercury after people from the world of the arts and literature —authors, painters, sculptors, poets, architects, etc.» But the working group didn’t know enough about these fields, «especially from an international perspective», and Morrison explained that «that is why reference works and univeristy researchers had to be consulted in order to elaborate a list of possible names».

In 1979 the group lead by Morrison aproved the incorporation of the name of Ausiàs March to the list, but said: «I don’t remember who suggested Ausiàs March, but all in the group recognised it was a good suggestion as an important writer of the Catalan language». As confesed to Jennifer Blue, from the USGS, answering to why the name of Ausiàs March for the crater, « I wanted to be sure of having Catalan and Castilian writers represented in the craters of Mercury».

## Features on Mars' Moons (Deimos and Phobos)

### 1. **Swift Crater** (Deimos)
- **Location**: Deimos, Mars' outer moon
- **Approval Year**: 1973
- **Namesake**: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), Irish writer best known for *Gulliver's Travels*
- **Note**: One of only two named craters on Deimos; authors who wrote about Martian satellites were eligible for naming convention

### 2. **Voltaire Crater** (Deimos)
- **Location**: Deimos, Mars' outer moon  
- **Approval Year**: 1973
- **Namesake**: Voltaire/François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), French philosopher, satirical novelist, historian, and playwright
- **Note**: Also one of only two named craters on Deimos; shared the same naming category as Swift

## Feature on Earth's Moon

### 3. **Lucian Crater** (Earth's Moon)
- **Location**: Mare Tranquillitatis region
- **Diameter**: ~6.85 km
- **Approval Year**: 1973
- **Namesake**: Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–c. 180 AD), Greek satirist and writer whose works include fictional and philosophical tales
- **Note**: Previously designated Maraldi B; named after the 2nd-century Greek satirist/author

---

These three craters are the complete list of features that:
1. Exist on Earth's Moon or Mars' moons
2. Share namesakes with pre-20th century literary figures primarily known for writing fiction or poetry
3. Had their names officially approved in 1973 by the IAU through the USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature
